analysis.one_liner: Cuts royalties, bids, and rent that oil and gas companies pay to drill on federal land.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would lower the royalty rate oil companies pay on federal-land oil and gas from 16.67% to 12.5% and cut minimum bids from $10 to $2 per acre, was introduced with 8 Republican cosponsors and has received no action beyond its committee referral.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the rules for oil and gas drilling on land owned by the federal government — meaning land whose minerals belong to all Americans. It would cut the royalty companies pay on what they extract from 16.67% to 12.5%, drop the minimum bid at lease auctions from $10 to $2 per acre, cut annual rent from up to $15 to $1.50–$2 per acre, and eliminate a fee companies currently pay to show interest in a lease. It would also let lands that draw no bids be leased without competitive bidding for a $75 application fee, and make it easier to reinstate canceled leases at reduced rates. The bill reverses royalty and bidding increases enacted in 2022.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies that lease federal land, and companies that want to lock up acreage cheaply. They would pay less for every barrel and every cubic foot of gas taken from public land, pay far less to hold leases they do not drill, and could acquire parcels no one bids on without competing for them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas companies on federal land

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the royalty rate on oil and gas produced from federal land from 16 2/3% to 12 1/2%, reducing what companies owe on every unit of production removed or sold [S2][S3].

Lowers the minimum bid for federal oil and gas leases from $10 per acre to $2 per acre and cuts annual rental rates from as much as $15 per acre to $1.50 per acre for the first five years and $2 thereafter [S2][S3].

Eliminates the fee for expressing interest in a lease and expands noncompetitive leasing: lands that receive no bids, and certain low-producing properties, could be leased without competitive bidding for a non-refundable $75 application fee [S2][S3].

Eases reinstatement of leases that were cancelled or terminated, at reduced royalty and rental rates, and extends noncompetitive lease terms to as long as 10 years plus continuation while production lasts [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who own the minerals on public land. Every point of royalty cut is revenue the Treasury — and the states that share in onshore royalties — does not collect, and noncompetitive leasing at $2 minimum bids and $75 fees lets companies control public acreage without paying what a market would charge.

drawbacks.text: The 2022 law this bill partially unwound raised federal onshore royalty and minimum bids precisely because the old terms were considered below market; this bill would return the onshore royalty to 12.5%, a rate lower than the pre-2022 standard of 12.5% only marginally below what competitive auction was meant to test [S3].

Noncompetitive leasing lets the first qualified applicant take land no one bid on for a $75 fee at a 12.5% royalty, removing the auction that is supposed to ensure the public gets fair value for minerals it owns [S3].

Supporters would argue lower rates and easier leasing encourage domestic production and energy independence, and that some marginal wells are only economic at lower royalties — but the bill lowers rates across the board, including on lands that would be leased anyway [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains go narrowly to companies leasing federal land; the cost is spread across every taxpayer in the form of foregone royalties and rents from publicly owned minerals. Lower prices at the pump are possible but indirect and unguaranteed, while the revenue loss and expanded noncompetitive access to public land are direct and certain.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, which has taken no further action on it, so it has not come anywhere near a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Andrew Ogles introduced the bill on January 16, 2025, with six original cosponsors, all Republicans [S1][S3].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources, which is the only action recorded since [S5].
Eight Republicans total are listed as cosponsors [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost — the bill is stalled in committee, which for now preserves current royalty and bidding terms for the Treasury.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury's current terms, so far

for.name: Rep. Andrew Ogles
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cut federal onshore oil and gas royalties, rents, and minimum bids.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and all 8 cosponsors are Republicans; no Democrat supports it in the record.

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies leasing federal land
industries.note: The bill cuts what they pay to extract publicly owned oil and gas and lets them acquire acreage without competing for it. Their gain comes directly out of royalty and rent revenue that would otherwise flow to the Treasury and to states.

analysis.trajectory: With only 8 cosponsors and no committee action more than a year into the session, the bill is very unlikely to advance; most bills referred to committee without leadership backing never receive a markup or a floor vote.
